text.p: The United States' largest health care provider, Columbia HCA Health Care Corp, is aiming to become a major player in the Australian health care system, the head of its new Australian arm says.

Geoff Sam, newly appointed chief executive of Columbia Health Care Australia, told Reuters the company would seek to acquire or partner private hospitals and to be involved in private investment in the public hospital system in Australia.

The company has substantial funds available to enter the market and currently is bidding for projects at public hospitals in Queensland (Robina and Noosa) and South Australia (Adelaide's Queen Elizabeth hospital), Sam said in an interview.
While the company had not yet made any acquisitions, negotiations and discussions were underway in different States which "may or may not come to anything," he said.
Sam, former chief executive at Adelaide's Ashford Community Hospital, said reports that Columbia had earmarked A$1.3 billion for Australian acquisitions came "from someone's imagination".
However, he said: "If you want to be a major player in health care, you have to have substantial funds to do it."
"Basically the intent of Columbia Health Care Australia is to either acquire or partner private hospitals to become a major health care provider in Australia," he said.

Sam said Columbia's strategy in Australia would reflect its success in the U.S. in the 'hub and spoke' approach to health care delivery, creating a network of hospitals which complement each other, from acute services through to home based care.

It would also depend on what acquisitions it was able to make, with the market already featuring a number of major players such as Mayne Nickless subsidiary Health Care of Australia, Australian Hospital Care Ltd, and the privately owned Ramsay Health care, he said.
"I think where Columbia have been successful in the U.S. and where we may be able to distinguish ourselves in the Australian market is to partner with not-for-profit hospitals," he said.
Sam said many of these hospitals, often run by religious groups, became caught up in the constant capital reinvestment required for modern acute care hospitals.

"So some of their original missions to take care of say the less privileged in society have been lost simply in the roundabout of maintaining the pace in acute health care for the privately insured," he said.

Columbia had been successful in the U.S. in providing equity injections which allowed these hospitals to provide real benefit returns to their particular communities through establishment of foundations or community trusts, he said.

On the public health front, Sam said most Australian state governments were now looking for some private sector interest in delivering at least co-located services, private health care and shared private-public facilities on public hospital grounds.
"We are going to look at the opportunities throughout Australia to be involved in any private investment in the public health sector," he said.
Sam said competition again in this sector was intense, but added: "I think the market is big enough for another major player."
